title: Printing in Three Dimensions
context:
Three-dimensional printing, also called additive manufacturing, builds objects layer by layer from a digital design. This contrasts with traditional machining, which cuts material away from a solid block. The first commercial machine, which used a technique called stereolithography, was patented in the mid-1980s by the American engineer Chuck Hull. For about two decades afterwards the technology was used almost exclusively to produce prototypes.

The expiry of several key patents around 2009 helped make cheap desktop printers possible, and a wave of publicity followed. Commentators in the 2010s predicted that most households would soon own a printer and make everyday objects at home. This did not happen. Printing even a simple item can take several hours, the quality of cheap plastic is limited, and for large quantities of identical goods conventional mass production remains far less expensive. Many early buyers also discovered that operating a printer demanded more patience and technical skill than the advertisements implied. Models had to be designed or downloaded, files repaired, and failed prints cleaned up, and a large share of the machines ended up unused in cupboards after the first few months. Even so, a small community of enthusiasts continued to share designs online, repairing and improving each other's machines and gradually raising the standard of what an inexpensive printer could produce.

The technology has instead found its place in specialised niches. In aerospace, an engine manufacturer redesigned a fuel nozzle that had been assembled from around twenty separate parts and now prints it as a single piece, which is lighter than the original. Printing is also well suited to products that are unique to each user. Hearing-aid shells and clear dental aligners, for example, are now almost always produced this way, because every ear and every set of teeth is different.

Medicine offers further possibilities. In bioprinting, machines deposit living cells in layers to build tissue, and researchers have succeeded in printing small pieces of cartilage in the laboratory. Complete organs with working blood vessels remain a distant goal, and none has been transplanted into a patient. More immediate progress has been made with prosthetics. Printed artificial hands for children can be made cheaply, which matters because children outgrow them quickly.

Construction firms in several countries have experimented with printing the walls of small houses from concrete. Critics point out that cement production has a high carbon footprint and that building regulations have not kept pace with the new methods. Metal printing, meanwhile, consumes large amounts of energy, and some of the fine powders used can be hazardous to breathe. Supporters argue that the process creates less waste, since material is added only where it is needed, and that spare parts can be printed on demand rather than stored in warehouses. Whether these savings outweigh the costs is still unproven.
